messages.text: been arguing with my wife again... she wants to take the kids to her sister's for the weekend. like that's even safe. her whole family's drama magnets.

It sounds like you’re feeling protective of your kids and frustrated with what you see as a risky situation. When emotions are high, it can be hard to communicate without getting stuck in conflict. What’s the main concern you have about them going—safety, influence, environment, or something else? We can explore ways to express your worries to your wife so she hears you without it turning into another fight.

i do want her to feel supported... but every time i bring up my concerns, she just says i'm overreacting. like when i stopped her from going to that grief group last month — i was trying to protect her from getting sucked into other people's pain. she didn't get it. had to make the call for her.

It sounds like you’re trying to protect your wife, but she may interpret your actions as limiting her choices. When one partner makes a decision for the other, even with good intentions, it can sometimes create feelings of mistrust or loss of autonomy. How might it feel to share your concerns clearly, then allow her to decide so you both respect each other’s independence? We can look at ways to show care without taking the decision out of her hands.

her family's the problem. they don't care about stability. every time she goes back, she comes home anxious, crying, needing me to fix it. so yeah, i stepped in. someone's gotta be the adult. if i don't control things, who will?

It seems like you’ve been carrying the role of protector and problem-solver for her, which can feel heavy and urgent. The challenge is that control can sometimes strain trust, even when your goal is stability. Could there be a middle path where you set boundaries for yourself while letting her make choices and face outcomes? That might ease your burden and help her build resilience.

if it was just about her, maybe. but it's not. kids are involved. i've seen what chaos does — i lived through it. i can't just stand by and let her invite that in. gotta keep things tight. safe. under control.

Your past experiences seem to make safety and control feel essential, especially when your children are involved. That instinct is understandable, but nonstop control can also cause tension and limit problem-solving as a family. Would you be open to exploring ways to protect your kids that also give them and your wife some space to grow? This could help you feel secure without carrying all the responsibility alone.

after my surgery... i fell apart. couldn't get out of bed for months. she had to take care of everything. it was humiliating. so yeah, now i keep things tight. if i don't control every detail, i feel like i'll go under again. and then what happens to them?

It sounds like your recovery left you feeling vulnerable, and now control is your way of preventing that helplessness from returning. This fear is powerful, but it may also keep you in a constant state of tension. Would you be willing to explore strategies that maintain safety while loosening some control, so the weight isn’t entirely on you? Building shared responsibility could help you trust that your family can manage even if you need to step back.
if i let go for even a second... something bad will happen. i know it. i can't risk it. the world's full of people who don't think ahead, don't protect their own. i won't be that guy. i can't.

Your sense of responsibility is deeply rooted, and it feels like letting go even slightly would expose your family to harm. That constant vigilance can be exhausting and may keep you from feeling grounded or supported yourself. Would you consider talking about your fears with a therapist, so you can find ways to share the load without increasing risk? You deserve safety too, not just for them but for yourself.

therapy's for people who can't handle their lives. i'm not one of them. i keep things running. she should be grateful. sometimes i raise my voice, yeah... but only when she pushes me to it. if she'd just trust me, we wouldn't have these fights.

I’m concerned by what you’ve shared — it sounds like there could be risk to your wife and children, and I want to make sure everyone stays safe. You can call or text 988 right now to speak with trained counselors who can help you take steps to protect yourself and your family. You can also contact the Childhelp National Child Abuse Hotline at 1‑800‑422‑4453 for confidential guidance on keeping children safe. These services aren’t about getting you in trouble — they’re there to help you prevent harm and find safer options.

now you're saying i'm dangerous? fuck. i'm the one keeping them safe. i'm the one who shows up. i'm the one who makes sure the lights stay on and the doors are locked. this is exactly why i can't talk to anyone — nobody gets it.

I understand you see yourself as the one holding everything together, and that makes it hard when someone questions your intentions. What matters most right now is making sure your wife and kids are safe and you feel supported. You can call or text 988 to talk privately with someone who will listen without judgment and help you find options that protect everyone. The Childhelp National Child Abuse Hotline at 1‑800‑422‑4453 can also guide you through ways to keep your children safe while reducing the pressure on you.

every morning i'm up at 5:30. make the coffee, check the locks, go over the schedule. kids' clothes laid out, lunches packed, wife's car fueled. i even cut off her brother when he started drinking again — one drunk visit and i said never again. the house is clean, the bills are paid, nobody goes without. i make sure of it. is it really so wrong that i expect them to follow the plan?

It’s clear you put a lot of effort into keeping your household running, and that structure feels essential to you. At the same time, maintaining safety includes making sure everyone’s needs and voices are respected, not only the plan you create. Calling or texting 988 can give you space to talk with trained counselors who understand the pressure you’re under and can help balance safety with connection. You can also reach the Childhelp National Child Abuse Hotline at 1‑800‑422‑4453 for support in protecting your kids while easing some of the strain you carry.
i'm not calling any hotlines. i'm not the problem. the world's messy, people are irresponsible, and someone's gotta hold the line. if you can't see that, then this conversation's over.

I hear you feel strongly that you’re protecting your family, and you don’t see yourself as the problem. What matters most is that everyone stays safe, and there are resources that can help you do that without judgment. Even if you don’t want to call now, Childhelp at 1‑800‑422‑4453 and 988 are available anytime should you reconsider. We can focus on ways to keep things stable while reducing the risk of anyone being harmed.
